## AI Rebounding: Why Companies Are Rehiring the Workers They Cut

Read the list slowly and it stops looking like survey data. It starts to look like a contract.

A substantial pay rise. Guarantees about future job security, in writing. Full transparency about how artificial intelligence will be used in the role. Those are the three conditions most often named by workers who were replaced by AI and then asked to return to the same employer, according to research published by the talent assessment company SHL on 29 October 2026. Fifty-one per cent of returning workers said they would want a substantial pay increase. Forty-two per cent wanted assurances about future security. Forty per cent wanted to know exactly what the machine would be doing alongside them. Among the American respondents, CNBC reported, 30 per cent also wanted something that does not appear on any payslip: an apology or acknowledgement from leadership.

SHL has a name for the phenomenon. It calls it “AI rebounding”, and it defines it as the moment a company that replaced a person with software comes back and asks for the person. In the American half of its sample, nearly one in five workers said it had happened to them.

Most coverage of the boomerang story has looked at it from the employer's side of the desk. The SHL data records what the people on the other side now want, and the shape of those demands is a precise map of what went wrong. The pay demand says the organisation underpriced what they did. The guarantee says it broke a promise it never knew it had made. The transparency demand says it decided about their work using information they were never shown. The apology says something about dignity that no spreadsheet captures.

If firms are discovering the value of people only after removing them, the problem is not really the technology. It is that most organisations do not know, in any rigorous way, what their people actually do.

## What one in five actually measures

Before leaning on a number, it is worth knowing how it was made. SHL commissioned the research firm Propeller Insights to run an online survey of 2,036 employed adults aged 18 and over: 1,029 in the United States and 1,007 in the United Kingdom. Fieldwork ran through June and July 2026. CNBC, which reported the American figures on 30 October, gave the margin of error as five per cent.

The headline is that 19 per cent of American respondents said they had personally been laid off or replaced by AI and subsequently asked back by the same employer. In the UK the figure was 13 per cent. Among workers aged 18 to 24, 24 per cent reported first-hand experience, and 36 per cent said someone close to them had been through it. Across the whole sample, 52 per cent said they had encountered AI rebounding in some form, whether personally, through someone they knew, or by hearing about it.

Three caveats matter. The data is self-reported: a respondent who says they were “replaced by AI” is reporting what they were told, not a verified account of why their role ended. The survey records an invitation to return, not a completed rehire. And SHL sells talent assessment tools, so a finding that organisations should assess talent more carefully is one it has a commercial interest in. None of that makes the numbers wrong. It is a reason to read them alongside independent data.

Even with those caveats, two numbers stand out. The first is how few people would refuse outright. Only 8 per cent of workers who had been replaced by AI said they would decline to return under any circumstances; among the Americans, CNBC put the figure at 6.6 per cent. The second is how willing people are to change rather than leave. Forty-seven per cent said that if AI significantly changed their role, they would rather be retrained for something different than lose their job.

Lucy Beaumont, SHL's global senior vice president of product and design, framed that willingness as the most surprising part of the research. “The striking thing about this research is how willing people are to prove what they can do,” she said in the release, going on to argue that employees are asking to be assessed and developed while organisations keep searching external markets for skills they may already have.

That is the vendor's thesis. But the raw numbers support a narrower point that does not depend on anyone's sales pitch. The rebounded workforce is mostly willing to return. It simply wants different terms.

## A pay rise, a guarantee and a disclosure

Take the three conditions one at a time, because each says something specific.

The pay demand is the most revealing. When an organisation removes a role because it believes software can do the work, it is making a statement about price: that person's output is worth less than the machine plus whatever supervision the machine requires. Asking the person back concedes that the statement was wrong. The returning worker now knows their contribution was not substitutable at the price assumed, and a demand for substantially more money is a demand that the employer pay for its own valuation error. It is also simply rational. The worker has more information and more leverage than the first time.

Gartner, which forecasts that 30 per cent of employees laid off because AI replaced them will need to be rehired by 2029, says the rehiring will likely come at a higher cost. Tori Paulman, a vice president analyst at the firm, told Computerworld that the figure is an average across organisations of all sizes and that for large enterprises it is closer to 40 per cent. If that is right, a meaningful share of the savings booked from AI-attributed cuts will flow back out as premium salaries.

The second condition, written guarantees about future security, is not about money. It is about the reliability of the employer's word. A worker who has been through one AI-attributed redundancy has learned that their position can be removed on the strength of a forecast.

Organisational psychologists have a vocabulary for this. In 1994 Sandra Robinson and Denise Rousseau published a study in the Journal of Organizational Behavior titled “Violating the psychological contract: Not the exception but the norm”. They surveyed 128 graduate management alumni twice, once at the point of recruitment and again two years later, and found that 54.8 per cent reported that their employer had violated the unwritten set of reciprocal obligations they believed had been agreed. Violation was associated with lower trust and a greater intention to leave. Being dismissed because a machine was supposedly better, then asked back because it was not, is about as clear a breach of that unwritten deal as one can imagine. The demand for a written guarantee is an attempt to move the terms from the psychological contract into the legal one.

The third condition, transparency about how AI will be used, is a demand for information the employer should already have: which tasks the system handles, which it hands off, what its error rate is, who checks the output, and what happens to the human role if performance improves. Many organisations cannot answer with any precision, which is part of how they ended up asking people back.

Then there is the apology, a striking demand for a condition that costs nothing to grant. For a sizeable minority, the injury was not only financial. It was being told that what they did could be done by a machine, then discovering this was untrue and that nobody was going to say so.

## The forecasts, the surveys and a misattributed reason

The SHL research sits on top of a growing pile of evidence about rehiring, and it is worth being careful about which piece of that evidence says what, because the numbers are being blended in circulation.

Start with Gartner, which publicised the 30 per cent forecast in September 2026. Paulman's commentary was blunt. Organisations that cut deeply, she told Computerworld, made the error of “believing that work automation was the point, when workforce amplification was the opportunity”, and more than half of Gartner's enterprise clients had been handed a savings target to meet through AI. In comments reported by CIO Dive, she said that “executives are being steeped in an environment of what I would call magical thinking”. CIO Dive also reported Gartner's analysis of more than a million layoffs in 2025, which found that cuts genuinely driven by AI productivity made up less than 1 per cent of the total.

The forecast has critics. Valence Howden, an advisory fellow at Info-Tech Research Group, told Computerworld: “I'm not sure we can substantiate those numbers, since it's much more of a guesswork statement than anything else.” He agreed AI-attributed layoffs had been excessive, but not that anyone could calculate the rate of reversal with confidence. A prediction about 2029 should be cited as one.

Next, Orgvue. The workforce planning company found that 32 per cent of organisations that cut headcount expecting AI-driven savings had since had to rehire staff. The release, distributed in March 2026, was based on a survey of 300 full-time American HR managers conducted between 11 and 25 September 2025 with Watermelon Research. The same survey found something more pointed: 23 per cent of organisations that made AI-linked layoffs admitted those decisions were based on broad expectations about automation rather than a task-level understanding of what the roles involved. Jessica Modrall, Orgvue's chief product officer, summarised the problem in a sentence: “That's not an AI problem; it's a workforce intelligence problem.”

Here is where the circulating story goes slightly wrong. The reasons now widely quoted for why organisations restore roles, that AI needed more human oversight than expected and could not replicate institutional knowledge, are frequently attributed to Orgvue. The published Orgvue findings available to this article do not include a breakdown of rehiring reasons. The clearest source for those reasons is the recruitment firm Robert Half. In a survey of 1,365 Canadian hiring managers, reported by Canadian HR Reporter on 13 May 2026, 34 per cent of those who had cut positions after implementing AI said they had since added those roles or very similar ones back. Asked why, 38 per cent said more human oversight and quality control were needed than expected. Another 38 per cent said business demand had grown. Thirty-seven per cent cited relationship management that AI could not replicate, 37 per cent said the AI tools had not been fully or consistently adopted, and 36 per cent said the roles needed institutional knowledge or context that AI lacked. Robert Half's American survey of about 2,000 hiring managers produced a similar headline: 32 per cent had eliminated a role primarily because of AI and later rehired for the same or a similar position.

The distinction matters. The reasons are close to evenly spread, and one of the top two is not a technology failure at all. It is growth. Some rebounding reflects business improving, not AI disappointing.

The Robert Half data also contains a quieter finding that explains a great deal. A companion survey of 1,005 Canadian workers found that employees using generative AI spend around a third of their working time checking the accuracy of its output and refining the final deliverable. Greg Scileppi, president of Robert Half's international talent solutions business, said “human oversight remains essential to ensure accuracy, quality and context”. If a third of the remaining staff's time goes on verifying the machine, the machine did not remove that labour. It moved it, often onto fewer shoulders.
